strengths: SFTMix addresses a relevant NLP problem with a concrete recipe: partition instruction examples by model confidence, interpolate response-token representations and labels, and add a weighted Mixup objective. It requires no additional response annotation.

The matched NTP comparisons show consistent improvements across Llama-3.1-8B and Mistral-7B on Alpaca and UltraChat. Table 1 reports approximately 0.20–0.29 higher MT-Bench scores and 0.32–1.67 percentage-point improvements in length-controlled AlpacaEval win rates. Medical QA results provide complementary evidence, with average accuracy gains of 1.33 and 1.66 percentage points.
The human evaluation provides evidence beyond automated judging: across 200 judgments on 80 instructions, SFTMix receives 42.5% preferences versus 26.5% for NTP, with 31% ties.

Experiments with a smaller reference model, LoRA, and selected training subsets demonstrate useful compatibility. The pipeline, interpolation rule, response-length handling, and principal full-fine-tuning hyperparameters are reasonably clear.
weaknesses: The decisive missing control concerns the central claim that training-dynamics-based confidence is crucial. There is no comparison against random pairing, within-confidence pairing, or confidence from a single checkpoint. Section 5.2 changes the training responses and does not compare confidence-based and quality-based pairing on that same modified dataset. Consequently, it cannot establish the necessity of confidence-based pairing over ordinary Mixup. The relationship to the cited cartography-based Mixup work of Park and Caragea (2022) also needs clearer differentiation.

The claimed mechanism exceeds the evidence. A t-SNE visualization of extreme-confidence examples and inspection of 100 examples do not demonstrate that confident examples overfit or that SFTMix improves generalization specifically for unconfident examples. Low perplexity can reflect task simplicity, while high perplexity can reflect legitimate response diversity or annotation noise. Confidence-stratified held-out measurements would support these claims; otherwise, they should remain hypotheses.

Evaluation uncertainty and model selection weaken confidence in the reported improvements. Appendix B.1 selects the regularization weight using MT-Bench and AlpacaEval-2, which also serve as final evaluation benchmarks; no separate development set is described. Results transferred to other settings partly mitigate this concern. However, independent training-seed results, confidence intervals, and paired significance analyses are not reported. Repeated evaluation rounds alone do not establish robustness to training variation.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite the supplied core hyperparameters. The manuscript provides no implementation link and omits the reference-checkpoint collection schedule, loss-reduction conventions, LoRA configuration, precise generation settings, and GPT-4 judge version. The human study also lacks sufficient information about annotators, presentation randomization, agreement, and aggregation of repeated judgments per instruction. These omissions matter when assessing relatively modest gains.

The practical efficiency claims are insufficiently quantified. The default procedure requires a separate reference-model fine-tuning run plus checkpoint scoring, but total compute, memory, and runtime are not reported. Smaller-reference and LoRA results demonstrate compatibility, while comparisons against inexpensive regularizers and a matched total-compute baseline would establish practical value. Taken together with the missing central controls and evaluation safeguards, these gaps leave the paper borderline for Findings despite its encouraging empirical consistency.
